newsitem.title: UK: Sterling's gain spurs downgrade pain for UK shares.
newsitem.headline: Sterling's gain spurs downgrade pain for UK shares.

text.p: A wave of downgrades spurred by sterling's strength battered more British stocks on Thursday as analysts continued to cut corporate profit forecasts and warned that further pain was on the way.

Britain's stock market has been flooded by downgrades this week because of fears that sterling's advance to its current dizzy heights will threaten exports and hit the foreign currency profits of British companies.
"There are certainly more downgrades to come," said Credit Lyonnais Laing strategist Corey Miller. "Some of the big overseas-earners will be feeling more pain before this is over."

Sterling has been selective in its victims -- many firms are relatively untouched or even boosted by a stronger domestic currency -- but British blue-chip stocks with overseas earnings are suffering as their exports and foreign operations are hit.
"Currency appreciation is a two-edged sword," Miller said. "Imports become cheaper which has benefits on the cost side so the overall market impact of sterling's strength is cloudy."
But London's headline FTSE 100 index of blue-chip shares -- which stood at 4,084.6 points, down 2.9 points at 1600 gmt -- would be damaged by the pound's advance, Miller said.

"The FTSE includes more international stocks so the weight of downgrades will probably outweigh the benefits," he said. "And even if a strong sterling isn't hitting earnings too badly, it has an effect on sentiment in certain sectors."
Robert Buckland, strategist at HSBC James Capel, stressed there was no simple relationship between the pound and the FTSE.
"The FTSE went up last quarter even though sterling was up. But sterling has certainly hit individual stocks," he said.
From a low of 84.0 in August, the trade-weighed index which measures sterling against a basket of major currencies climbed to 96.1 by the year-end, a rise of more than 14 percent.
It has continued to climb, reaching a four-year high of 96.5 on Thursday, and analysts say no near-term easing is expected.

"Things might calm down once we see a rate hike, on the basis that we've risen ahead of the event and might calm down on arrival," Buckland said. "But if people expect further rate rises, sterling will be off to the races again."

British Steel has been among the hardest hit. Its shares fell to a 12-month low on Thursday after Merrill Lynch, SocGen and NatWest halved profit forecasts for the year ending March 1998. "British Steel is always vulnerable. You'll see it move almost point-for-point against sterling," Buckland said.

The chemicals and drugs sectors also took a battering. Analysts at James Capel said they were cutting profit foreCasts for the chemicals sector in 1997 and 1998 by around 4.5 percent because of sterling's strength, prompting ICI and BOC shares to fall. Courtaulds also weakened.
NatWest was reported to have cut 1997 earnings estimates for drugs firms Glaxo Wellcome, Zeneca and SmithKline Beecham on Wednesday.
It also shaved its forecasts for building materials firms RMC Group and Wolseley, again on the basis of currency appreciation.

"We've found the sectors which are most vulnerable to a strong pound are health, household products, pharmaceuticals and chemicals," Miller said. "General retailers and brewers tend to be unscathed and most financials are also undisturbed."
Analysts said hedging could take the sting out of sterling's advance for some companies. "A lot of these companies will be using derivatives which will soften the blow," Miller said.
"We could see sterling weaken also as an election approaches, so we won't be too aggressive sellers of currency-sensitive stocks," he said. "But I don't think this is over yet."
